name: The Back Room
caption: A liminal-horror adventure for 5th–8th level characters
description:
The party beds down in the storeroom over a tavern kitchen and never leaves it. Stairwells, stables, corridors and campsites — all the back room, misremembered — and in there with them, their own first characters, who want the game to go on forever.

Contents: 43 scenes with walls, lights, notes and Monk's Active Tile Triggers automation; 22 actors; 54 journal entries; 5 roll tables; 3 playlists; a SoundBard macro.

Start with the journal 00. The Back Room: Adventure Overview; the journal folder is a Campaign Companion campaign with three prepared Sessions.

A blank-faced copy of one character: the one with the fewest Misremembering changes so far (the corridor has taken the least from them). It steps out of the far door on the second pass through the Corridor Between. It has that character's sheet with every number halved and no name.

Running it. This block is a 5th-level adventurer halved and plays as written; or run the macro The Back Room: make the Echo of a character to make a halved copy of a real character. It acts right after the copied character. The full procedure is on the Room 3 journal, The Echo. It stops the moment the loop breaks.

description.value: The Echo's statistics are the mirrored character's with every number halved (Hit Points, Armor Class, attack bonuses, damage, save DCs). As written, it is a 5th-level adventurer halved.

The Echo acts immediately after the character it copies. On round 1 it does nothing. From round 2, on its turn it repeats that character's previous turn: it moves to the square they started that turn in and takes the same actions at the same squares, with every number halved, against whatever is in those squares now. It copies everything, including healing, dodging and doing nothing. If the party goes through the far door, it steps out of the next far door at the start of the following round.
The Echo cannot be reduced below 1 Hit Point while the Corridor Between is looping. When the loop breaks it stops where it stands, and is not there a moment later.
[[/attack extended]]. [[/damage average extended]]. Uses the mirrored character's main weapon damage, halved.

Bartleby Stickit, Bart to his friends (which is everyone who has drunk his cider twice). Keeper of the Stickit Inn, as his father was. Kind. Tired in a way that is not unhappy. He pours the house cider with a heavy hand, led the party up the stairs with a lantern and showed them the cots, and in the night he comes down the wrong stairwell with a tray.

Room 1. He tells them it is not morning yet and they should go back to bed; the road will be there tomorrow. He knows one detail about one character that the character has never told anyone. If pressed about it he does not understand the question.

Room 5. His voice from the common room below is the sound of ordinary morning.

description.value: Bartleby never attacks and cannot be made to. If attacked he sets the tray down, says 'well', and goes back up the stairs. He will have set a second tray by morning.

Once, in Room 1, he mentions one detail from a character's backstory that the player has never said aloud at the table: pick it from the sheet before the session. With nothing on the sheet to use, he asks after the character by the name the player almost gave them.

Asked whether he used to be a scrivener, he nods: 'But I'm not any more.' Asked why, or asked to write, copy, check or witness anything at all: 'I would prefer not to.' He says it pleasantly, every time, and goes back to wiping the mug.

Room 2. There is a hooded stranger in every booth, and every one of them is a role, repeating the hook word for word. None of them is the Remnant.

Room 5. The stranger's voice rises from the common room below, asking Bart whether the party is up yet. The job is still there.

description.value: The stranger offers a plain, ordinary job: ride guard on a wagon of lamp oil over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross, three days, forty gold a head, half tonight, leaving at first light (the handout The Job). It is never a trick, and if the party leaves at the end, it is still there to be done.

scenes.name: Vista: Corridor: Hallway of Inn Doors

text.content:
The Back Room

The Back Room is a liminal-horror adventure for four to five characters of 5th to 8th level, run over two or three sessions. The party meets at the Stickit Inn, a roadside tavern famous for its cider, played completely straight. They take the hook, buy provisions, and bed down in the storeroom over the kitchen before the dawn road. They never leave that room. The whole dungeon — stairwells, stables, corridors, campsites — is the storeroom, misremembered.

The thing in there with them is not a monster. It is the first party: each player's first-ever D&D character, as the table misremembers them — overpowered, cooler than they were, one running joke swollen into a whole personality. These are the Remnants. They are not hostile. They want the game to keep going, forever, with the party in it.

The message, in one line: the places you are most comfortable are the ones you never finished leaving.

Theme: Unfinished

One word, chosen first. Every room is something that was never finished — a story cut off, a character who never levelled, a campaign that died in the spring. 'Liminal' describes the dressing; 'unfinished' is the point. When you improvise a detail for a room, ask what in it was left undone.

Content Notes

Isolation, time loss, having one's memories quietly edited, a copy of a character, and a warm place that does not want anyone to leave. No gore. Talk with your players before you start about anything they'd rather fade to black.

Sound

Automatic. Every scene and vista has an ambient loop as its scene sound (playlist Back Room: Ambience): it starts when you activate the scene and stops when you leave. The Corridor copies share their place's loop. The landing scene comes in already active, so after importing click Activate on it once to start its music. The door tiles play their own stingers.

By hand. Back Room: Music has a track for each beat that wants one (Session 1 tavern, the Corridors, The Cover, the Echo, the Hoard fight, dawn, the Last Word); most of the adventure is better with ambience alone. Run the macro The Back Room: set up SoundBard once per GM browser to fill a SoundBard bank with the cues: the door, a door closing somewhere, footsteps a half-beat late, the X, the lantern lighting itself, the waterfall that stops when someone speaks, a horse, the Remnants laughing through the door, Fred's POW!, Rorvik bursting in, a monster waking, Strider's arrow.

The ambience and music come from four audio modules this one recommends (Ivan Duch's Music Packs, Michael Ghelfi Studios Audio Pack, SoundFx Library, Adventure Music); without them those sounds are silent and everything else works.

The Shape of It

The spine is a Five-Room Dungeon, but the five rooms are destinations, not neighbours. The party reaches each one by wandering the Corridors: a pool of eight in-between places behind random doors, where no door ever leads back. Five fixed beats threaded through an unfixed maze.

BeatRoleScene
1Entrance / Guardian@UUID[Scene.lpscmZZIlhgEYct6]{The Back Room} — the storeroom over the kitchen; the barkeep as a gentle gate
2Puzzle / Roleplay@UUID[Scene.uKyO8AvTiuT8ys4Y]{The Common Room} — every patron is a role; find the Remnant among them
3Trick / Setback@UUID[Scene.KVQF67B2Q8tZP4pt]{The Corridor Between} — the corridor takes something from the party
4Climax@UUID[Scene.DhFbGAUmoWaedMdE]{The Hoard} — the first party, assembled, wants to finish the game
5Reward / Revelation@UUID[Scene.lpscmZZIlhgEYct6]{The Back Room} again — open the door or stay

The central gimmick, escalating: misremembering. Early, the rooms are misremembered. Middle, the party's own past starts to be. Late, the party meets the misremembered versions of themselves and has to decide whether to leave them behind.

Tone curve. Early rooms are off by one detail (comic, uncanny): the sword in the stone is a spoon. Middle rooms are wrong in ways that implicate the party: a barkeep who knows things the characters never said aloud. Late rooms stop pretending: the Remnants are in the room, and they are glad to see you.

The Library Layer

The players at this table began playing D&D in the upstairs room of a library: a reading room with pointed arches, dark timber ribs, two tall stained-glass windows in arched bays, a stained-glass lantern in the ceiling, green-painted wainscoting, armchairs round a low table, and an inner glass-walled room with double wooden doors and bookshelves. That room is the memory the whole adventure is built on, so the dungeon gradually becomes it: one detail in Room 1, one more per Corridor visit, a step per segment in Room 3, and in Room 4 the Hoard is the reading room. It is the misremembering, surfacing.

If your table did not start in a library, swap in the room where they did start — a basement, a kitchen table, a dorm lounge — and ladder its details the same way. The steps are in the Corridor rules.

Every book is a half-page book

Wherever the library layer puts a book or a shelf, every volume is one half-page long. This is a global rule, not a room's trope. Never explain it.

When a player opens one, roll on @UUID[RollTable.s5y6739k0kQfPWox]{the Half-page Books table} (or pick): each result links to a short handout to show them. Books 1–4 fit anywhere, 5–7 from visit 3 (each nods to one of the Remnants), 8–11 from visit 5, and 12 belongs on the shelves of the Hoard's inner room.

Goal & Progression

The stated goal arrives in Room 2: the Remnant hands the party a map with an X and says it marks the way out. It points at the Hoard. From then on the players can say what they are doing — follow the X — and the X pulls them through the Corridors.

The real goal is discovered in Rooms 4–5: the way out was the door they came in by. The stated goal was the thing keeping them from it.

Progression rule. Every Corridor scene has one door that can carry the X; the X moves between scenes when nobody looks at the map. The X door leads to the next fixed room, but it only appears once the party has done what the previous room required: found the Remnant in Room 2; left something behind in Room 3. All other doors are pool doors. Random doors for wandering, one scripted door for progress.

Pacing (2–3 sessions)

  • Session 1: Rooms 1–2 and two Corridors (visits 1–2).
  • Session 2: three or four Corridors (visits 3–6, including The Cover and the glimpse), then Room 3.
  • Session 3 (or the back half of 2): a Corridor at visit 7+ with a Remnant in it, Room 4, Room 5.

The Corridors are the pacing valve: add loops when the table is enjoying the dread, cut them when it isn't. Levels 5–8 is the right tier on purpose: past local nobodies, not yet legends. The characters are in a transition whether the players have noticed or not.

text.content:
How to Run It: Step by Step

The whole adventure in the order you run it, with the Foundry pieces each step uses. The room journals have the detail; this is the thread through them. Each session also has a Session page (Campaign Companion) with the same plan in one paragraph.

Three habits for the whole adventure

  1. Doors move the party and activate the scene. The first character onto a door tile takes the whole party to the new scene, and that scene becomes the active one (its ambience starts and everyone's view follows). The exceptions are the Hoard's exit, where characters leave one at a time (activate Room 5 yourself once they are all through), and any scene you open by hand.
  2. NPCs and monsters are already on the maps. People who arrive mid-scene are placed as hidden tokens (GM-only): Bartleby by the landing in The Back Room, the Echo near the third segment's far door, Rorvik in the Hoard's inner room, Strider in every C copy of the Corridors. Right-click a token and toggle its visibility when they appear.
  3. GM controls are hidden tiles. They sit in the top-left corner of a scene. Switch to the Tiles layer to see them; double-click one (from the Tokens layer) to fire it. The full list is in @UUID[JournalEntry.ZIYvT56dW0zzwxND]{02. Automation}.
  4. Keep a tally sheet with three lists: the visit count (every Corridor scene entered, including repeats); Misremembering changes (who, what it was, what it is now); and what each character left behind in Room 3. Rooms 4 and 5 use all three.

Before the first session

1. Check the modules

Required: Monk's Enhanced Journal, Campaign Companion, Monk's Active Tile Triggers. Recommended for sound: Ivan Duch's Music Packs, Michael Ghelfi, SoundFx Library, Adventure Music, and SoundBard. Without the sound packs the adventure runs silent but works.

2. Read three journals

The overview, the rules (they are the theme: Misremembering, the Signature, no door leads back, leaving something behind), and the automation table.

Use

  • @UUID[JournalEntry.uYYbQcluL0y0VHqf]{00. The Back Room: Adventure Overview}
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.5T3hjUmGMhmAPUbl]{01. Rules of the Back Room}
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.ZIYvT56dW0zzwxND]{02. Automation (Monk's Active Tile Triggers)}

3. Prepare the people

Read @UUID[JournalEntry.WQLxmK3fXBuHwyxp]{The Remnants} and swap in your own table's first characters if this isn't the original table. For @UUID[JournalEntry.HDjGNHIrowvpCC8M]{Bartleby Stickit}, pick one secret detail from each character's backstory (Room 1, The Guardian). Decide which player is the latecomer, if any.

Use

  • @UUID[JournalEntry.WQLxmK3fXBuHwyxp]{The Remnants}
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.Bz6oCPNCrHvHDm9i]{Cast}
  • Each Remnant's Person page links its actor.

4. Set up sound

Run the macro The Back Room: set up SoundBard once (Macro Directory: the folder icon at the left end of the hotbar). It fills two SoundBard banks: Corridors and People. The playlists Back Room: Music and Back Room: Stingers are there for anything else.

Use

  • Macro: The Back Room: set up SoundBard
  • Playlists: Back Room: Ambience, Music, Stingers

5. Set the opening

Make the landing scene active and click Activate on it once so its music starts. Place the player tokens on the cots in The Back Room scene, out of sight until you need them.

Use

  • Scene: Welcome: The Stickit Inn (navigation: The Stickit Inn)
  • @UUID[Scene.lpscmZZIlhgEYct6]{The Back Room} (navigation: Upstairs)

Session 1: Rooms 1–2, Corridor visits 1–2

6. While players arrive

The landing scene is up and the Stickit Inn's music is playing. Nothing to do.

Use

  • Scene: Welcome: The Stickit Inn

7. The evening at the Stickit Inn

Narrate the inn and the job, played completely straight: @UUID[JournalEntry.OtOUVhSExtP4SOGO]{Kael Shadowmere} in the corner booth, three days to Thistlecross, forty gold. Show the handout. If you want a picture on screen, activate the vista of the common room for a moment. Start the music track Session 1: A Cozy Tavern.

Use

  • @UUID[JournalEntry.mnmkjsUJYJ6rVeHB]{Room 1: The Back Room} (The Evening)
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.cAqtiEcEW9UEFGbK]{Handout: The Job}
  • Scene: Vista: The Common Room (optional)

8. Upstairs to the back room

Activate @UUID[Scene.lpscmZZIlhgEYct6]{The Back Room} and read the boxed text. If a player is late, run The Latecomer: their character arrives last, with Bartleby and a candle.

Use

  • @UUID[Scene.lpscmZZIlhgEYct6]{The Back Room}
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.mnmkjsUJYJ6rVeHB]{Room 1: The Back Room} (The Latecomer)
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.HDjGNHIrowvpCC8M]{Bartleby Stickit}

9. The night event

Someone wakes; the lantern is lit. The stone in the corner has a hilt in it: when a player clicks the stone, that player gets the Toothless Key handout automatically. Bartleby comes down the stone stairs with a tray and asks them to go back to bed (The Guardian is not a fight).

Use

  • @UUID[JournalEntry.mnmkjsUJYJ6rVeHB]{Room 1: The Back Room} (The Night Event, The Guardian)
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.CV7to52Qcd6eYan0]{Handout: The Toothless Key} (opens itself from the stone)
  • SoundBard: The lantern lights itself

10. Into the Corridors (visit 1)

When a token steps onto the stairwell or the hayloft door, it is sent to a random Corridor scene. Activate that scene. Open the matching Corridor journal and use its visit-band cue (nothing yet at visits 1–2). Tick visit 1.

Use

  • @UUID[JournalEntry.UiR8fvzzRUCSQvD6]{The Corridor Pool: rules for every place}
  • The Corridor journal for wherever they landed (Stairwell, Stable, Hallway, Clearing, Market Row, Crossing, Crossroads)
  • @UUID[RollTable.4NjmmaNof9d3nLv7]{the Corridor Pool table} if you'd rather choose by roll

11. Visit 2, and the way to Room 2

Any door sends them somewhere else in the pool; tick visit 2. When you are ready for Room 2, double-click GM: Reveal the X door → Room 2 in the scene they are in: the X appears on one door. Walking through it takes them to the Common Room.

Use

  • GM control (any Corridor scene): Reveal the X door → Room 2

12. Room 2: the Common Room That Isn't

Activate @UUID[Scene.uKyO8AvTiuT8ys4Y]{The Common Room}. Every patron is a role. Roll the drunk's joke once and repeat it forever. One patron is real: @UUID[JournalEntry.EjLE1kpe2J4MbyeP]{Fred the Fighter}. When he says his Signature, click his table: everyone gets the X Map. End the session on the map.

Use

  • @UUID[Scene.uKyO8AvTiuT8ys4Y]{The Common Room}
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.3AaqWvvfQSAFBMcV]{Room 2: The Common Room That Isn't}
  • @UUID[RollTable.EH7rPdsPvHwTYLOu]{the Drunk’s Joke table}
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.EjLE1kpe2J4MbyeP]{Fred the Fighter}
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.5XTLcFdNQL0mKlgF]{Handout: The X Map} (opens itself from Fred's table)
  • SoundBard: POW! (Fred)

Session 2: Corridor visits 3–6, Room 3

13. Back into the Corridors

The common room's far door leads into the pool. Every arrival resets the fog and whispers you the band. Visits 3–4: sound (footsteps a half-beat late). Visits 5–6: a glimpse. Use each place's own cue first, then the generic table. Books on a shelf are half-page books. Each short rest in a Corridor costs a Misremembering.

Use

When the table needs a real fight, double-click GM: Next door → The Cover instead of letting them roll a door. The six monsters are frozen; stepping into a person-shaped gap wakes one (the tile whispers which). The cave's exit puts them back in the pool; nothing from the treasure pile survives it.

Once they have the X Map, double-click GM: Reveal the X door → Room 3 in the scene they are in. The X door takes them to the Corridor Between.

17. Room 3: the Corridor Between

Activate @UUID[Scene.KVQF67B2Q8tZP4pt]{The Corridor Between}. Walking forward loops through six identical segments. Teach the rule with the clue ladder, one clue per pass. On the second pass @UUID[JournalEntry.9at7iDHrSzf8jO4A]{The Echo} steps out of the far door (the tile reminds you). When someone sincerely leaves something behind, double-click GM: Loop Break, apply the Setback (one Misremembering), and ask whether anyone else wants to leave something too. Session 3: visit 7+, Room 4, Room 5

The far door of Room 3 puts them back in the pool, now at visit 7 or more: a Remnant is in the room. Reveal @UUID[JournalEntry.xn6e8Rm0P5t6onQ0]{Strider}'s token: it is already in every C copy, hidden, beside the X-door slot. He is not hostile; he wants the game to go on.

20. Room 4: the Hoard

Activate @UUID[Scene.DhFbGAUmoWaedMdE]{The Hoard}. The reading room, fully arrived; the Remnants are waiting in the inner room. The fight starts when someone makes it start. Rorvik's chair is empty: at the top of round 2 he bursts in (“Sorry I'm late. What did I miss?”). The Remnants can't be beaten: they stand back up. At the top of round 3, spell out the stakes and double-click GM: Open the way back: the glass doors they came in by now lead out. Use

21. Room 5: the Back Room, again

The glass doors bring them back to The Back Room with the fog kept: they never left. The toothless key opens the door at the top of the stairs. Double-click GM: Reveal if you want to un-hide the Corridor scenes' real names. Offer the choice: leave or stay. Use the tally: the Misremembering list and what each of them left behind.

Use

  • @UUID[Scene.lpscmZZIlhgEYct6]{The Back Room}

  • SoundBard: Remnants laughing, through the door

22. The Last Word

Out of character, after the choice: stop the ambience, start The Last Word: Sad Strings (Playlists: Back Room: Music), let it play a few bars, then put the dice down and read the closing to the players. Then stop.

Use

  • @UUID[JournalEntry.xeoMFbrUveFZwBiv]{Room 5: The Back Room, Again} (The Last Word)
  • Music: The Last Word: Sad Strings

Afterwards

To clear the adventure out of a world, run the macro The Back Room: remove the adventure from this world. It asks first, then deletes exactly what the adventure imported, itself included, and leaves your own documents alone.

Rules of the Back Room

Four rules carry the theme. They are for you, not the players: each one is discovered at the table — the first rewritten detail, the first door that opens on somewhere else, the first thing left behind. Say the rule aloud only after the table has met it.

  1. Misremembering. Each short rest taken in a Corridor rewrites one small backstory detail of one character — a sibling's name, the colour of the house, which god. The GM changes it on the sheet and tells only the other players. Roll on @UUID[RollTable.01EqhTgCZWRqmaFt]{the Misremembering table} for what changes, or pick. Track every change (who, what it was, what it is now): Room 5 needs the list.
  2. The Signature. A Remnant's one remembered thing auto-succeeds once per round, no roll, no save. Everything else about it is blank. A finished character has a whole sheet; an unfinished one has one line.
  3. No door leads back. Every door in the Corridors sends the party somewhere else in the pool, never to the place they left (not even another copy of it). The one scripted exception is the Room 4 exit. The visit counter escalates what is in there with them.
  4. Leaving something behind is the only way forward. Something the player chooses and does not get back: an item set down, a slot spent on nothing, a story told once and never again. It is required once, to break the Room 3 loop; it is what the Remnants are made of; and it is the choice in Room 5. Never gate it on a keyword; reward the first sincere sacrifice the table invents. What counts, what doesn't, and the clues that teach it are in Room 3: Leaving Something Behind.

The Corridors

The Corridors connect the five rooms and are where 'stuck' happens. Three rules run them.

1. No door leads back. Every door the party uses sends them to a random Corridor scene from the pool, never the scene they left. In Foundry the door tiles do this: the first character through a door takes the whole party with them, all to the same place, set down on separate squares. The GM only watches.

2. Something is in here with you — by visit count. Track how many Corridor scenes the party has entered in total (keep a tally; on each arrival the tiles reset the fog and whisper you the band reminder, but they do not count).

VisitsCueLibrary layer
1–2Nothing. Furniture is wrong by one detail.A strip of green wainscoting on one wall.
3–4Sound: footsteps matching theirs, a half-beat late. A chair creaks in an empty room. (The Cover is reached from a pool door in this band or the next.)Doors become double wooden doors with glass panels; through one, bookshelves.
5–6Glimpse: a figure at the end of the corridor, gone when looked at directly. It is wearing something one of the players' first characters wore.A pointed arch; a stained-glass lantern-window on a landing; carpet on stone.
7+A Remnant is in the room. It is glad to see you. It does not attack.Timber ribs overhead. The room is half library now.

3. Rest costs memory, not hit points. Short rests work normally, but each one taken in a Corridor applies Rule 1 (Misremembering).

The pool (d8). Stairwell, stable, hallway of inn doors, campfire clearing, market row at closing, ferry crossing, crossroads at dusk, cellar (from visit 5 only). Roll on @UUID[RollTable.4NjmmaNof9d3nLv7]{the Corridor Pool table} if the tiles are not doing it for you. One misremembered trope per place — never two; one is uncanny, two is a joke. The places are written up in 06. The Corridor Pool.

Remnants

GM prep (done for this table)

Each player was asked privately: What was the first D&D character you ever played? Name, class, and the one thing everyone remembers about them. Their answers are the five Remnants below. For a different table, ask the same question, don't say why, and rebuild the five from the answers; a player with no answer gets a fallback Remnant.

Building a Remnant.

  • Take the first character's class and build it at the party's level using the standard NPC approach, or a sidekick-style block if you'd rather keep it light.
  • Max hit points. No rolling.
  • The Signature. The one remembered thing becomes a feature that always works: once per round, it auto-succeeds, no roll, no save. The barbarian who was 'just really strong' always hits. The rogue who always rolled nat 20s on Stealth is simply not there until it chooses to be.
  • Everything else is blank. The Remnant cannot answer any question about its past that isn't the Signature. It doesn't know its hometown. It knows it had a tragic backstory but not what it was.
  • It never attacks first. It wants the game to continue; it will fight if that's what the party wants to do.
  • It stands back up. At 0 HP it rises at the start of its next turn, in the pose it fell in, with full HP, and continues mid-sentence.
  • It cannot leave a room through a door the party came through. That is the only hard limit on it, and it is the exit mechanic for Room 4.

This table's Remnants.

  • @UUID[JournalEntry.EjLE1kpe2J4MbyeP]{Fred the Fighter}: his player isn't sure he ever played him; he was certainly a comic strip in a summer-camp newspaper, briefly. Signature: POW! (one hit a round lands, at maximum, lettered in the air). He is the Remnant in Room 2: the player who doesn't remember playing him is the one who will recognise him.
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.FnjKc1XDXbKsWpEI]{Thon}: half-elf wizard with a Rod of Lordly Might. Signature: the rod is always the right tool. He remembers every button and no spells.
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.B2W0zbujemjBh92N]{Rorvik}: half-elven magic-user and thief, longsword, a hothead. Signature: always acts first. His player usually ran the game, so nobody remembers his adventures, including him.
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.U6yyMf1DxqYCG5Lc]{T. Morlock}: halfling thief-acrobat, 7th level. Signature: every acrobatic move works. He has his character sheet; nobody knows what the T. stands for.
  • @UUID[JournalEntry.xn6e8Rm0P5t6onQ0]{Strider}: a ranger built out of a beloved novel. Signature: knows the way. He is the Remnant who surfaces in a Corridor at visit 7+, and he offers to lead (always toward the Hoard).

Fallback Remnants for a player who misses a session, or for another table: @UUID[JournalEntry.RSMjDexanOtXtRnA]{Raven Nightshade}, @UUID[JournalEntry.DbKnx325wVNC2Fhq]{Grukk Skullsplitter}, @UUID[JournalEntry.AGV5L6xZVIw9oCCb]{Mordecai the Magnificent}.

Using them. Fred appears in Room 2. Strider surfaces in the Corridors at visit 7+. All five are in Room 4. They are filed under People, never Monsters.

Automation with Monk's Active Tile Triggers

This module requires Monk's Active Tile Triggers (MATT). Doors are tiles; walking onto one moves the token (and its owner's view) to another scene. Monster tokens never set them off. Every tile is named in its MATT settings, so you can find and adjust any of them from the Tiles layer.

GM Controls

Hidden GM control buttons sit in the top-left corner of scenes. Switch to the Tiles layer to see them, then double-click one from the Tokens layer to fire it.

SceneControlWhat it does

Any pool sceneNext door → the CellarSends the party to the Cellar copy with this scene’s letter. The Cellar is never in the random pool; use this from visit 5.
Any pool sceneNext door → The CoverSends the party to the cavern. Once, at visits 3–6.

The Back RoomRevealA reminder to un-hide the pool copies' real names for the moment in Room 5.

Automatic Tiles

WhereTriggerEffect
Pool scenes, each doorEnterDoor cue; the whole party (every player character's token on the scene) goes to one random arrival in another place, in the same copy as this scene (A, B or C). Never another copy of this place, never the Cellar. The party always arrives together.
Pool scenes, each arrivalEnterFog is reset for everyone and the GM is whispered the visit-band reminder. Tick the visit counter by hand (the tiles remind you; they do not count).

The library climbs on its own. Each Corridor place has three copies, A, B and C, each one step more library. Which copy the party is in is the stage of the adventure, and it only ever climbs: the night doors in Room 1 lead to A copies; the Common Room’s door and The Cover’s exit lead to B copies; Room 3’s exit leads to C copies; and every Corridor door leads to another place in the same copy. So visits 1–2 are in A, visits 3–6 in B, visit 7+ in C, and nothing to count or switch. Each place’s X-door control works in whichever copy the party is in.

Tips. Cross-scene moves bring each token's owner along, so move the whole party before switching your own view. Pool copies are hidden from the navigation bar and share bland names on purpose; the Reveal moment in Room 5 is when to un-hide them. If a tile misfires, toggle its Active checkbox in its config.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.pfm6KZbSlr8JKy2C]{the vista} (a painted view of the room, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 1: The Back Room

The Stickit Inn sits where the Kettle Pass road leaves the valley, and everyone for three days in any direction knows its cider: pressed in the yard, served cold in clay mugs, stronger than it tastes.

Play the cliché straight and let the players relax into it. @UUID[JournalEntry.OtOUVhSExtP4SOGO]{Kael Shadowmere} in the corner booth has a job: ride guard on a lamp-oil wagon over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross — three days, forty gold each, half now, leaving at first light (the handout The Job has the terms; swap in your own hook if your campaign already has one). The party takes it, buys provisions, and @UUID[JournalEntry.HDjGNHIrowvpCC8M]{Bartleby Stickit} leads them up the stairs from the common room to the storeroom over the kitchen, where they can sleep before the dawn road.

Why they're here

The adventure never says, on purpose: you all meet in a tavern is the oldest opening in the game, and playing it straight lets the players relax. If your table wants a reason, pick one (or roll a d4):

  1. It's on the road. The inn sits where the Kettle Pass road leaves the valley: the last bed and hot meal before three days of high road. Anyone going over the pass stops here.
  2. The cider. Everyone for three days in any direction knows the Stickit's cider. Someone in the party has been promising the others a mug for weeks.
  3. The job brought them. Word has gone round the nearby towns: guards wanted for a wagon over the pass, ask at the Stickit Inn. They came to answer it.
  4. Your own campaign. They are passing through on the way to wherever they were already going, and this is where night falls.

For a table that started playing together long ago, the cliché is the point: this is how the first party met, too.

What the party already knows about the road is in the handout The Kettle Pass: give it to them before the session, or let Bartleby and the stranger hand it out a line at a time.

The barkeep goes up ahead of you with the lantern. A short landing at the top of the stairs, a door, and the storeroom: shelves of sacks and crocks, a cot for each of you already made up, one lantern on a hook, a small window over the yard. He sets the lantern down and tells you he'll have bread on at first light, and a jug of the house cider for the road.

Describe it in loving, mundane detail. Let them count the cots. In the window, one pane of coloured glass that was not there at supper. Nobody comments on it; the GM does not either.

Keyed areas

  • A1. The landing. Top of the common-room stairs. The door to the storeroom.
  • A2. The cots. One per character, along the left wall, blankets turned down.
  • A3. The shelves. Provisions, with the party's receipts tucked under the crocks. Behind the far unit, a door nobody has noticed yet.
  • A4. The window. Small, four panes. One of them is coloured.
  • A5. The stone. In the corner by the chest: a stone with a hilt in it.

The Latecomer

At this table one player usually arrives late (the player whose first character is @UUID[JournalEntry.B2W0zbujemjBh92N]{Rorvik}), and session one will be no different. Plan for it rather than around it: their character is the last guest of the night at the Stickit Inn, and the rest of the party meets them in the back room.

Footsteps on the stairs, and a second light. Bartleby comes up with a candle and someone behind him, travel-stained, apologising. 'One more for the road, if you'll have them. Came in on the last of the light.' The last cot, you notice, was already made up.

Run the introductions by lantern light, in character, as the others are bedding down; the newcomer has heard about the job from the stranger downstairs and is in. If the player arrives after the night event has begun, they are the one who wakes: they arrive in the dark, Bartleby is not with them, and the lantern is already lit. A late arrival is the best possible way into this adventure.

The Night Event (the Insomnia Rule)

Someone wakes. Pick the character whose player is most likely to get up and look.

The lantern is lit. Nobody lit it. The door to the landing is open a hand's width and the stairs beyond it are stone, going down — the stairs you came up, but too many of them, and no light at the bottom where the common room should be.

Behind the shelves (A3), a second door nobody noticed: it opens into the hayloft over the stable, with a ladder down. This is how the storeroom connects to the yard; it also seeds the Stable in the Corridor pool, and it is the riddle door (see the Corridor Pool, Stable).

The first anchor object. The stone in the corner (A5) has a hilt in it. Whoever pulls draws out a long iron key with no teeth. It opens nothing in the room. Keep it; it matters in Room 5. Give the handout The Toothless Key.

Automation

Automated: the stairwell and loft doors send tokens into the Corridor pool; clicking the stone opens the key handout.

The Guardian Is Not a Fight

@UUID[JournalEntry.HDjGNHIrowvpCC8M]{Bartleby Stickit} comes down the stone stairwell carrying a tray. He is kind. He tells them it's not morning yet and they should go back to bed; the road will be there tomorrow. He knows a detail about one character that the character has never told anyone — pick it from a sheet before the session. If pressed, he doesn't understand the question.

The test here is only whether the party chooses the stairwell (or the loft ladder) over the cot. If they go back to sleep, they wake in Room 1 again, and the barkeep has set a second tray.

Leaving. Whichever way they go — down the stairwell or down the loft ladder — the first door at the bottom is a Corridor door. Visit 1 begins.

journal.name: Room 2: The Common Room That Isn't

pages.name: Room 2: The Common Room That Isn't

text.content:
Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.aWw0Z8nmdJOkzlVB]{the vista} (a painted view of the room, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 2: The Common Room That Isn't

The Stickit Inn's common room. The fire is lit, the tables are full, and nobody is looking at you. In every booth, a hooded stranger. The barmaid is walking a slow circle between the tables with a tray and has not arrived at one. A drunk by the hearth is telling a joke to nobody.

Every patron is a role: a hooded stranger in every booth, a quest-giver who repeats the hook word for word, a barmaid who walks in a circle and never arrives, a drunk who says the same line no matter how many times you talk to him. Guards at the door say there's nothing to see here. There's a lot to see here.

Keyed areas

  • B1. The booths. A hooded stranger in each, offering the job in the same words.
  • B2. The bar. Nobody behind it. Mugs of the house cider, full, every one the same pale gold. One is a different colour.
  • B3. The hearth. The drunk, and his one line: roll on @UUID[RollTable.EH7rPdsPvHwTYLOu]{the Drunk’s Joke table} the first time anyone talks to him, then tell that same joke, word for word and with the same pause, every time after.
  • B4. The door. Two guards. 'Nothing to see here.'
  • B5. The stairs. Up to a landing that is not the landing they came down.

The Puzzle

One patron is not a role. It is the first Remnant, @UUID[JournalEntry.EjLE1kpe2J4MbyeP]{Fred the Fighter}: one player's first character, misremembered (and possibly never played at all; he was certainly a comic strip). It doesn't know it's in a tavern. It thinks it's mid-adventure and the party are old companions. The puzzle is social: figure out which patron is real, and get it to say the thing everyone remembers it for (its Signature). When it does, the room goes quiet and every role turns to look at the party.

Three clues, so the table can't miss it:

  1. The Remnant is the only patron who asks the party a question.
  2. It is the only one whose cider is a different colour: red as wine, where every other mug in the room is pale gold.
  3. The player whose character it is will recognise it from the description before anyone else does — let that player sweat before they say so.

Payoff. The Remnant gives them a map with an X. The X moves when nobody looks at it. It is pointing at the Corridors. Give the handout The X Map. From this moment the X door can appear in the Corridors (the GM's X-door tile).

The roles, in their own words

Every role has one line and says it exactly the same way every time, whoever asks and whatever they ask. Never improvise past it; the repetition is the horror.

RoleTheir line
A hooded stranger (every booth)“Lamp oil, over the Kettle Pass to Thistlecross. Three days. Forty a head, twenty tonight, the rest on delivery. We leave at first light.”
The barmaid (walking her circle)“Just coming, love.” (She never arrives. Step into her path and she walks round you, still smiling, still coming.) With the Patrol module installed she walks her circuit round the middle table by herself while you are on this scene; Patrol's walking-figure button in the token controls stops and starts her.
The guards at the door (B4)“Move along. Nothing to see here.” (Both together. Ask what they are guarding: “Nothing to see here.”)
A merchant at a table“Finest wares this side of the pass! Have a look!” (There is nothing on the table.)
An old man by the window“In my day, the pass was a dangerous road.” (Ask how: “In my day, the pass was a dangerous road.”)
The drunk (B3)His one joke: roll once on @UUID[RollTable.EH7rPdsPvHwTYLOu]{the Drunk’s Joke table}, then the same joke forever.

When Fred says his Signature, every role stops mid-line and turns to look at the party, all at once. Hold it for a beat. Then they go back to their lines, a little quieter.

The way out

  • The door (B4) is the way on. Before the Signature the guards stand in it (“Nothing to see here”); after, they step aside together without a word. The door tile sends the party into the Corridors, copy B.
  • The stairs (B5) go up to a landing, a door, and the bottom of the same stairs. Every time. Let them try twice.
  • If they leave without the map (they fight past the guards, or Fred never says it): let them. Fred turns up in the next Corridor they enter, a beat behind them, out of breath: “You forgot this!” He gives them the map there.

The X Map in play

The handout is a picture of a maze of rooms with an X on it. It is how the players feel they are following something, while the doors stay random. Use it like this:

  • When they look at it in a Corridor, the X is never on the room they are in. It is a room or two away, in a direction you choose: ahead, left, past the stairs. If they go that way, the next room is somewhere else entirely, and the X is a room or two away again. Describe it plainly each time.
  • It only moves when nobody is looking. If a player says they keep their eyes on it, it stays perfectly still, and nothing changes. The moment they fold it away, or look up, it has moved.
  • The X door appears when they look away. When you are ready for the next room (Room 3 after the map, Room 4 after Room 3 and Strider), wait until nobody is looking at the map, fire GM: Reveal the X door, and then let them look: the X is on the room they are in, on one of its doors. One of the doors now has an X on it, too.
  • Strider can read it. At visit 7+ he glances at it and says “That's two doors from here”, and he is right, because you make him right.

Automation

Automated: click the Remnant's table when the Signature is said to hand out the X map; then use GM: Reveal the X door in whichever pool scene the party reaches next.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.K2wx1qmvyXXsdJ3K]{the vista} (a painted view of the room, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 3: The Corridor Between

A corridor ten feet wide with a door at the far end. Torches lit ahead, dark behind. The door behind you is locked, and you can see the key for it hanging on a nail beside the far door.

Two doors: the near one is locked and its key is behind the far one. The far one opens onto the same corridor, from the other end.

The trick. Walking forward loops. In Foundry the loop is not a teleport: the map is a strip of identical segments and the party simply walks on (see Automation). Each pass is one step more library — ribs overhead, then the green paint, then the pointed arch at the far door — which reads as progress, and is: the corridor is going somewhere.

Breaking it. The loop breaks on any sincere act of leaving something behind — a treasured item set down, a spell slot spent on nothing, a story a player tells about their first character and then agrees never to tell again. Don't gate it on a keyword; reward the first real sacrifice the table invents. When it breaks, the GM fires the Loop Break tile and the next far door is the exit. What counts, what doesn't, and how the table works it out are on the next page.

Segments

C1–C6. Six identical segments in a line. Each far door is a tile that lets the party into the next segment. Segment dressing ladders the library: C1 plain; C2 a scratch on the wall at hip height and a dropped coin; C3 green wainscoting; C4 a glass double door with a bookshelf behind; C5 a pointed arch; C6 ribs overhead. Attentive players notice the scratch at the same height and the coin back on the floor.

Automation

Automated: each far door walks the party into the next identical segment. Fire GM: Loop Break when something is left behind; the next far door becomes the exit, back into the Corridors.

Leaving Something Behind

This is the one thing the adventure asks of the players, and it should feel like a choice, not a password. Here is how to judge it, and how they find out.

The test

It counts when all three are true. When in doubt, ask the player one question: “Is that for good?” If the answer is yes, and it costs them to say it, it counts.

  1. Chosen. The player decides, for their own character. Nobody can leave something behind on someone else's behalf.
  2. It costs. The character, or the player, will miss it. It is something they would otherwise use, carry, or tell.
  3. It stays. It is left in the corridor, and nobody goes back for it or gets it back later.

Counts

  • A thing that matters. A named weapon, a holy symbol, an attuned magic item, a backstory keepsake (the ring, the letter, the father's sword), a real share of the party's gold. Set down on the floor and walked away from.
  • Power spent on nothing. A spell slot of the character's highest level, or a once-a-day feature (Rage, Channel Divinity, Wild Shape, a Ki or Sorcery pool), spent into the empty corridor with no target and no effect. The player says aloud what they are giving up.
  • A story told once. A player tells the table a real memory of their first character, or of an old session, and agrees never to tell it again. (The GM can keep it; it turns up in Room 4.)
  • Part of who they are. A title, a vow, a nickname, a backstory detail. The player picks it and lets it go; apply it like Misremembering, except they chose it.

Doesn't count

  • Junk. A torch, a copper piece, a ration, a rock. The corridor gives it back: it is lying on the floor of the next segment, in the same spot, like the coin.
  • Anything taken back. Picked up again, fetched with Mage Hand, recovered later by any means. If they go back for it, the loop resumes.
  • Loopholes. An illusion of an item, a conjured or summoned object, a decoy, a “loan”. The corridor is not fooled, and neither is anyone at the table.
  • Resources spent for a reason. A spell cast at the Echo, a potion drunk to heal, a feature used to scout. That is play, not leaving.
  • Someone else's sacrifice. An NPC's belongings, a familiar dismissed on another character's say-so, another player's item.
  • Hit points or blood. Bodies heal. The Back Room does not take what comes back on its own; rests cost memory here, not hit points.

When it breaks

The first sincere act is enough: fire Loop Break. Then pause before anyone opens the far door. The corridor is quiet; the torches behind them have gone out. Ask whether anyone else wants to leave something too. Nobody has to, but each character who does gets the Room 5 boon tied to what they left. (The Echo, if it was fighting, vanished when the loop broke.) Note who left what: the Remnants in Room 4 have every one of those things, and Room 5 asks about them again.

How the players figure it out

Never tell them the rule. Let the corridor teach it, one clue per pass through the far door, and stop as soon as someone tries something.

PassClue
1Nothing but the loop. Let them test it: walk back, try the locked door, check for secret doors. Each segment is a little more library, which reads as progress.
2The scratch at hip height and the dropped coin are back, exactly as they were. Anything they dropped or used as a marker is back too. The corridor returns what nobody wanted. The Echo steps out of the far door: a copy of the character the corridor has taken least from, with no name and nothing in its hands.
3By the far door, a row of hooks that wasn't there before, each holding something a stranger left: a child's wooden sword, a wedding ring on a string, a folded letter with the wax unbroken, a dice bag. None of it can be taken; a hand passes through. One hook is empty for each character. (Narrate it; the hooks are not on the map.)
4A voice through the far door, warm and familiar (a Remnant, though they don't know it yet): “Everybody leaves something. That's how we got in here.” Then laughter, and nothing.
5+Each character remembers, in their own way, a rule from childhood: nothing goes through for free. Tell each player privately what their character half-remembers paying to get past something once (a toll bridge, a ferry, a lost tooth under a pillow). If they still have not tried anything, let the Echo take a thing from the character it copies, and break the loop on that — the corridor has taken its due, and that character gets no boon in Room 5.

Things that seed it earlier

  • The Ferry crossing in the Corridors: a jetty with no water and no ferry, the toll post empty. People expect to pay the ferryman.
  • The half-page book On the Proper Keeping of Inns: a free night is never free.
  • Fred in Room 2 wears things that are not his: a ring, a scarf, a holy symbol from some other party. He doesn't know where they came from.
  • The Remnants themselves are the answer, seen backwards: they are what people left behind.

The Setback

Whatever was left behind, a Remnant now has. And the corridor has taken something it wasn't offered: one character's bond, ideal, or a named person from their backstory is now subtly different, and only the other players notice. Apply Misremembering to one character now, chosen by the GM, and tell the others (@UUID[RollTable.01EqhTgCZWRqmaFt]{the Misremembering table}: use 4, 11, 14 or 15, or reroll until one comes up). This is the point where misremembering stops being about the rooms and starts being about the party.

The Echo

On the second pass through the far door, a blank-faced copy of one character steps out of it: @UUID[JournalEntry.9at7iDHrSzf8jO4A]{The Echo}. It is that character with nothing given up and nothing left: a sheet with every number halved and no name. It is the fight that tells the table the corridor wants something from them.

Who it copies

The character the corridor has taken the least from. Look at your tally: the character with the fewest Misremembering changes so far. If that is a tie, pick among them the one whose player has held on hardest (the one who refused a rest, kept every item, never told a story about their past). Anyone who has already left something behind in this room is never chosen.

Setting it up in Foundry

  1. Before the session (or at the table), run the macro The Back Room: make the Echo of a character and pick the character. It makes a new actor, The Echo of that character: their token art tinted grey with no name, their size, speed and ability scores, and copies of their equipped weapons and their spells with every number halved (hit points, AC, attack bonuses, damage and healing, save DCs). The base Echo is left alone, so you can make another.
  2. Drag that actor onto the scene at the far door the party just came through. Its attacks and spells roll from its own sheet, already halved.
  3. No time for the macro? Use The Echo as it is (a 5th-level adventurer halved) and give its token the character's art.
  4. Roll initiative. The Echo acts immediately after the character it copies, every round.

Running it: it repeats their last turn

  • Round 1. The Echo does nothing. It stands at the door in the pose the character is in, and moves when they move. Let the table look at it.
  • Every round after. On its turn the Echo takes the copied character's previous turn again: it moves to the square the character started that turn in, and makes the same attacks, spells and actions at the same squares, with every number halved. It does not choose targets; it hits whatever is standing in those squares now: the character, an ally who moved in, or nothing.
  • You only track one character. When the copied character finishes their turn, note what they did and which squares it touched. That is the Echo's next turn. A token marker or a quick drawing on each square helps.
  • It copies everything. A heal heals whoever is in that square. A shove shoves. A Fireball comes back on the same point at half damage. If the character took the Dodge action, the Echo dodges. If they did nothing, it does nothing.
  • It cannot be killed while the corridor loops. It never drops below 1 hit point. Damage still shows: let it crack and blur, but it stays standing.
  • Doors don't help. If the party goes through the far door, the Echo steps out of the next far door at the start of the following round.

How it ends

Only when the loop breaks: the moment you fire Loop Break, the Echo stops where it stands and is not there a moment later. That is the point of the fight. The party cannot win it, so it pushes them to work out what the corridor wants. Watch for the copied player realising that every attack they make comes back at the party a round later. When they stop attacking, the Echo stops too, and the corridor goes very quiet: that is the best moment for the next clue on the ladder. And if the copied character is the one who leaves something behind, and spends their highest spell slot into the empty air, say, the Echo copies that too, into nothing, before it goes.

If the table is struggling

  • Half damage keeps it survivable, but if the party is in real trouble, have the Echo copy a turn the character spent healing or dodging.
  • Point at the mirror: describe the Echo's swing as exactly the character's swing from a moment ago, same angle, same grunt. The player should feel it is theirs.
  • Never let it drop a character to 0 more than once. It is pressure, not a killer.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.XysYgliTG5K3KoUt]{the vista} (a painted view of the room, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 4: The Hoard

A dragon's hoard with no dragon. And the room is the upstairs reading room, fully arrived: pointed arches and dark timber ribs overhead, the stained-glass lantern in the ceiling, two tall stained-glass windows with dawn behind them, green wainscoting, armchairs. The hoard is the ring of armchairs round the low table, and on the table, where the coins should be, are dice — warm, as if they have just been rolled.

The dark lord's tower, painted, hangs between the arches where a portrait would; it is the same size it has been from every window. At the far end, the inner glass-walled room with the double wooden doors: through the glass, bookshelves, and the Remnants, seated, waiting for the session to start.

Keyed areas

  • D1. The glass doors. The party enters through them. They are the exit, later.
  • D2. The armchairs. The hoard. Dice on the table, warm.
  • D3. The portrait. The tower, between the arches.
  • D4. The inner room. Bookshelves of half-page books. The Remnants, and one empty chair.
  • D5. The windows. Dawn. The same dawn as Room 5.

The Antagonist's Motive

The Remnants are here, the full first party, all but one: Rorvik's chair is empty. They have been waiting for the boss. They think the party is the boss, or the rescue, or the sequel — it changes mid-sentence. What they want is simple and sympathetic: for the session to not end. They were never given an ending; they are offering the party the same.

The Fight That Can't Be Won

Remnants have max HP and their Signature always works. Dropped to 0, a Remnant stands up at the start of its next turn in the same pose it fell in. Beating them rebuilds the room (the load-bearing boss, in reverse). Spell the stakes out at the top of round 3: the players should understand that winning is the loop.

Rorvik is late. @UUID[JournalEntry.B2W0zbujemjBh92N]{Rorvik} is not in the room when the fight begins. At the top of round 2 the inner room's double doors bang open and he strides in, longsword already out:

'Sorry I'm late. What did I miss?'

From that round on he acts first, every round, as if he had been there all along. (His player will know exactly why.)

How it starts

The Remnants never attack first, so nobody draws a sword. Instead, when the party comes through the inner room's doors, the Remnants stand up, delighted, and Fred says it for all of them: “You made it! Right. Everybody roll initiative.” They think the party is the boss, or the rescue, or the sequel, and that it's time to play.

Ask everyone to roll initiative, for real. The combat tracker is the session starting. That is the trap: once the rounds begin, they want them never to stop.

What the Remnants do on their turns

Until someone attacks them, they play, not fight. Each turn, a Remnant does its Signature at the room, the way a player shows off a favourite trick:

  • Fred: swings at nothing; POW! hangs in the air over the low table.
  • Thon: presses a button; the rod becomes a ladder up to the timber ribs, or a ram against a bookshelf, and he looks round to see if anyone saw.
  • T. Morlock: vaults onto the back of an armchair, runs along the top of a bookshelf, lands on the table among the dice without disturbing one.
  • Strider: stands by the glass doors, looking at them, saying nothing. Someone has to notice where he's standing.
  • Rorvik (from round 2): acts first, every round, and wants to know what's happening.

If the party attacks, the Remnants fight back, gladly: this is the game. Signatures land, nobody stays down, and the room rebuilds itself round them. Make every hit feel like a good session: cheering, mock outrage, someone shouting a rule. It is the happiest fight in the adventure and it cannot be won.

If the party never attacks, the rounds still pass: talk, temptation, offers. The Remnants pull out chairs, roll dice for them, ask what their characters' names are. Rorvik still arrives at round 2. The way back still opens at round 3.

Round 3: the stakes

At the top of round 3, stop and say it out of the fiction, plainly: they can't be beaten; beating them is the loop. The doors you came in by are open now. Walking out is the only way to end this. Fire GM: Open the way back.

How It Actually Ends

The glass double doors the party came in by (D1) now lead back the way they came — the first time in the adventure that's been true. Combat ends the moment a character walks through them without looking back. Remnants will not follow. They will call after the party by the players' real character names from Room 1, and then by the first characters' names, and then stop. The Room 4 Exit tile sends the party to Room 5.

Without looking back

  • Each character walks out on their own turn. Before a player moves their token onto the doors, ask once: “Do you look back?”
  • If they don't, they step through and are gone (the tile takes them).
  • If they do, they stop on the threshold (keep the token just short of the doors). They see their own first character's chair pulled out for them, and a Remnant mouthing their first character's name. Nothing else happens. They can try again next turn.
  • Anyone left behind when everyone else has gone can still walk out; the Remnants won't stop them. But ask the question again, each time.

Automation

Automated: fire GM: Open the way back at the top of round 3; the glass doors then send tokens to Room 5 with the fog kept.

text.content:
Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.pfm6KZbSlr8JKy2C]{the vista} (a painted view of the room, no grid), then pull them to the map.

Room 5: The Back Room, Again

The storeroom over the kitchen. Dawn light under the landing door, and through the small window — which is now, entirely, a stained-glass window — the colours of the reading room laid across the cots. The cots are made. The lantern is out. The stone in the corner has no hilt in it.

This is the Room 1 scene with the fog kept and the same entry square: let Foundry tell them. The toothless key from Room 1 fits the door at the top of the stairs.

The revelation. They never left. Say it plainly through the environment, not a monologue: provisions still on the shelf with the receipts the party paid for, the hooded stranger's voice rising from the common room below, ordinary morning noise, and under it, pages turning. Fire the GM Reveal tile now if you want the players to see the whole shape of it in the scene list.

The Choice

Two doors, and each one is an answer. Nobody has to say the word choice: the room says it.

  • The landing door (A1): leave. The door at the top of the stairs is locked, and the toothless key from Room 1 turns in it. Beyond it, ordinary stairs, the right number of them, and the common room in the morning.
  • The hayloft door (A3): stay. The second door, behind the shelves: the riddle door from the night. Through it, from the hayloft, the Remnants, laughing (SoundBard: Remnants laughing, through the door, or the Stingers playlist). It is the only time the riddle door does not ask its riddle. It says, quietly: “Oh, it's you. Go on through. They kept your seats.”

Making it a real choice

  • Each player chooses for their own character. Not a party vote. The party can split, and it is allowed to.
  • Let each Remnant ask its own player. Through the loft door, one at a time, use their Room 4 lines (on their Person pages): Fred's “Same time next week?”, Strider's “The road can wait.” Speak to the player, not the character.
  • Put a real price on leaving. Read out the tally: every Misremembering change stays changed, every thing left behind in Room 3 stays left, and the Remnants will be gone. Leaving is the healthy choice, and it costs.
  • Put a real gift in staying. Staying gives everything back: every changed detail is as it was, everything left behind in Room 3 is on the cot, the party is whole, and nobody ever has to say goodbye to anyone. Say so plainly. It is not a trick.
  • Don't lean. No music cue, no meaningful look, no hint that one answer is right. Let the silence go on longer than is comfortable. The back room is warm; outside it is a cold morning and a long road.
  • Make it physical. On three, each player puts a hand on the table (stay) or a die in the middle (leave). Or have each player move their token: to the landing door, or to the loft door.

If they leave

The key turns as if the lock had been waiting for it. The stairs down are wooden, and there are fourteen of them; you count. The common room smells of bread. Bartleby is behind the bar in his apron, wiping a mug that is already clean, and he looks up and says, “There they are. Bread's hot. Jug's by the door.”

In the corner booth, the stranger has his hood down. He is younger than you thought, and he is checking the straps on a pack. “Wagon's in the yard,” he says. “If you're still coming.”

Outside, it is a cold, clear morning. The wagon smells of lamp oil and wet rope. The Kettle Pass road goes up into the hills exactly the way roads do, one bend at a time, and nobody has to count the bends.

Somewhere behind you, an upstairs window catches the sun. Just glass. All four panes clear.

Then the mechanics: each character who left keeps the changed details as they are now, gains a level, and gets one boon of your choice tied to what they left behind in Room 3 (a character who left a holy symbol finds their faith sits lighter and surer; one who spent a story finds people listen when they speak). The Remnants are gone. The toothless key is gone from every pocket.

Any character who stayed is simply not at the bar in the morning. Bartleby sets out one fewer mug and does not say anything about it, and neither does anyone else.

If they stay

The hayloft is warm and full of lamplight, and there is a table up here that was never in any hayloft: a low table, and chairs round it, and the people you used to be already sitting down. Someone has rolled dice. They are still warm. There is a chair for each of you, and a character sheet on each chair, and the name at the top is the one you almost gave them.

Nobody asks whether you are ready. Somebody says, “Right. Where were we?”, and nobody remembers, and it doesn't matter.

The campaign ends here, and it is allowed to be a good ending. Every session is session one. Tell the players that in those words.

Then, The Last Word

When the last character has gone through a door, stop the scene's sound (Playlists sidebar: stop Back Room: Ambience) and start the track The Last Word: Sad Strings in the Back Room: Music playlist. Let it play for a few bars. Then put the dice down and read The Last Word.

The twist, for the GM only

The back room is still there, under every tavern the party ever starts in. Any future campaign at this table can open with the barkeep setting out a tray.

The Last Word

Whichever way the party chose, close the campaign out of character: put the dice down, look up from the screen, and say this to the players, not their characters. If the party stayed, it lands harder: the characters stay in the back room; the players go home.

Over the years, this game has been our interstice: our liminal space. We pause our busy lives, the ones where we hurtle from one thing to the next, and make room around a table to weave stories about things that don't exist.

After tonight it's back to the real world, and whatever the next destination is, good or bad.

There have been times when being in the back room, playing this game, was better than real life. There have been times, I think, when all of us thought it might be better just to stay in that back room.

But our time here is done now. Time to go back.

Then stop. Don't recap, and don't explain the ending. Let the table sit with it, and let whoever wants to say their first character's name one last time say it.

text.content:
The Corridor Pool

Eight in-between places, one misremembered trope each. This is the spec the maps are built from; where it disagrees with anything else, it wins.

  • One trope, one wrongness. Never two — one is uncanny, two is a joke.
  • Three copies, and the library climbs. Each place is three Foundry scenes (A, B, C), same map, hidden from the navigation bar, all named with the place's bland name. Copy B is one step more library than A, copy C one more than B; the library steps are the only difference between copies, and the wrongness is in all three. The copy letter is the stage of the adventure and only ever climbs: Room 1's night doors lead to A copies (visits 1–2), the Common Room's door and The Cover's exit to B copies (visits 3–6), Room 3's exit to C copies (visit 7+). Every Corridor door leads to a different place in the same copy, chosen at random. Nothing to count or switch: the further in they are, the more the rooms look like the library.
  • Every book is a half-page book.
  • Entry doors. Each map has two or three doors. The random-door tile uses all of them as exits (never to another copy of the same place); arrivals are placed inside whichever door the tile chose, so a revisit can start from a different door. One door per scene is the X-door slot: a plain pool door until the progression condition is met, then the X appears on it and it leads to the next fixed room.
  • Darkness 0.6–0.8 on every Corridor scene; one or two light sources at most. Small vision is part of the concealment.
  • Size. 12×10 to 16×14 squares. Places to pass through, not explore.

The library steps

StepDetail
1A strip of green-painted wainscoting on one wall, chair-rail height.
2A door (or the door) is now a double wooden door with glass panels; through the glass, a bookshelf.
3A pointed arch where a square frame was; a small stained-glass lantern-window high in a wall; carpet over stone or dirt.
4Dark timber ribs overhead, meeting in a point. The room is half library now.

Copy A = the place's base step (0 for most). Copy B = base + 1. Copy C = base + 2. The generic cues (footsteps a half-beat late; a figure at the end of the corridor) apply anywhere; each place's own cues are below.

Visit 7+: the Remnant in the room

After Room 3 the party is in C copies, and every place's 7+ cue puts a Remnant in the room. The first is always Strider; after that, use whichever Remnant suits the place (Thon on a stair, Morlock on a rafter, Fred at the fire). Place the token, and play it from its Person page.

  • Strider, the first time. His token is already in every C copy, hidden beside the X-door slot: reveal it. He is in the room when they arrive, back to the wall, hood up, and he speaks first: “You're lost. Don't argue. I know these halls.” He knows their names. He offers to lead.
  • If they follow him, he walks to a door without hesitating. Wait until nobody is looking at the map, fire GM: Reveal the X door → Room 4, and the X is on the door he is standing beside. He holds it open: “After you.” He does not come through. In the Hoard he is already in his chair.
  • If they don't, he doesn't argue. In the next room they enter, he is already there, by a door, waiting: “This way.” Each refusal costs a visit, nothing else. Reveal the X door when you're ready either way.
  • The others, after Strider. A Remnant in a C copy is glad to see them, does not attack, and is on its way somewhere: “Session's about to start. You coming?” It leaves by a door the party didn't come through, and is in its chair in the Hoard.

Indoors to outdoors: going through

A door in the stairwell opens onto a crossroads at dusk; a gap in the trees round a campfire leads into a stable. Don't explain it, and never apologise for it. The Corridors are the storeroom misremembered, and memory joins places the way dreams do: by feeling, not by floor plan. What makes it uncanny instead of silly is that every crossing is described the same way, plainly, as if it were obvious.

  • Every way out is a door. Outdoors, the doors are still doors: the arches at either end of Market Row, the door standing on its own at the end of the ferry jetty, and where a path or a road leaves the map (the clearing, the crossroads, the ferry path) a door frame standing on its own, open, with light coming through it. Going through any of them, describe a threshold: a step over something, a change of air, a latch under the hand, even where there is no latch.
  • Say it in three beats. What they step through; one sense that changes; where they are. “You duck under the stable's yard door. The smell of hay goes, all at once, and there's woodsmoke. You're standing at the edge of a clearing at night, and the door behind you is a gap between two pines.”
  • The way back is never there. When they turn round, what they came through is the right shape for this place: the door they opened is now a gap in the trees, an arch, a road. Fog is reset on every arrival, so Foundry agrees with you.
  • Weather doesn't follow them. Outdoors is never quite outside. No wind on the skin, no rain, a sky with no stars or a dusk that never finishes. Indoors after outdoors, nobody's boots are wet. Let a player notice it.
  • Time does follow them. It is always the same night. A character who checks finds their candle the same length, their tea still warm, the moon (when there is one) exactly where it was.
  • Some crossings have a seam. Where it fits, keep one thing from the place they left for a beat: the stairwell's echo carrying on into the stable for a step or two; the clearing's firelight on their backs as they enter the hallway, then gone. One detail, never more.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.BrEuwFLlisNJAHRO]{the vista} (a painted view of the room, no grid), then pull them to the map.

1. Stairwell

Scene copies: @UUID[Scene.pilefMC8vBTXlYrl]{Stairwell}, @UUID[Scene.gnK7WIzDgZnU69q6]{Stairwell}, @UUID[Scene.KSzCpPkn1yXxv7Q6]{Stairwell}.

Trope. The dungeon stair; the inn's back stairs.

Wrongness. The steps go down and arrive one floor up. Three flights, two landings; the party descends and comes out above where they started, every time.

Map. A stone stairwell in section-as-plan: three flights around a square well, two landings. Entry doors: bottom (arrival), top (arrival), one landing door. 14×10.

Library base step. 0. (B = wainscoting on the landing walls; C = the landing door becomes the glass double door, bookshelf behind it.)

VisitsCue
3–4A footstep on the flight above, matching the last step someone took.
5–6A figure on the landing above, gone when the party arrives there.
7+A Remnant sitting on a step, delighted.

Dressing line. One half-page book on each landing, face down, as if someone stepped out for a moment.

Vista

On arrival, show the players @UUID[Scene.suYbtM5tAEK1Prtb]{the vista} (a painted view of the room, no grid), then pull them to the map.

2. Stable

Scene copies: @UUID[Scene.7lMGC0NCn8sVogBm]{Stable}, @UUID[Scene.uZuhqQUMQaOog2D9]{Stable}, @UUID[Scene.tJZXm4K8LGJt5yKP]{Stable}.

Trope. The party's mounts; the stable behind the inn.

Wrongness. The horses face the wall. They are the party's own mounts, saddled — the ones they never bought.

The loft door is the riddle door

This place is entered from the hayloft above; the ladder down is the door into the stalls. The hayloft door — the one behind the shelves in Room 1 and the loft door in every copy — speaks, as the two guards of the old riddle, one who always tells the truth and one who always lies. There is only one door. It cannot get the riddle right, contradicts itself mid-riddle, apologises, starts again. It opens the moment anyone tells it which guard it is; either answer works; it is grateful. (It is on the way in, not in the room, so it is not a second wrongness.)

The riddle door, in its own words

Its voice comes from the wood, about head height: polite, earnest, and a little out of breath, like someone reading from a card they wrote years ago and can no longer read. Play it as two voices that keep collapsing into one.

The Cover

The one honest fight, at Corridor visits 3–6. It is monsters, not Remnants — misremembered ones — and it is the payoff of the 'something is in here' escalation before the Remnant appears at visit 7+. Scene: @UUID[Scene.3VIIh9ZBk64Wr8UV]{The Cavern}, entered once, by the GM's scripted door at the visit of your choosing.

The table's first Monster Manual had a cover: a red dragon, a unicorn, a centaur, a troll, a roper and an owlbear, all in one fight with adventurers in a dark, treasure-filled cavern. Monsters with no business being together, and the first treasure hoard these players ever saw.

A pool door opens onto a cavern. Treasure heaped against the far wall, lit from a crack above. And in the middle of it, six monsters, mid-fight — a red dragon rearing, a unicorn with its horn lowered, a centaur drawing a bow, a troll mid-lunge, something like a stalagmite with its arms out, an owlbear — all perfectly still. They are fighting nobody. There are gaps in the picture the shape of people, and a dropped sword where one of them stood.

The monsters do not acknowledge the party. They keep fighting nobody, as they have since 1977. The thing in the room is busy; the party has to decide whether to interrupt it.

Trigger: stepping into a gap. Each gap wakes one monster — the one that was fighting whoever stood there — and only that one. The rest keep posing. The party chooses how much of the cover to fight. Two or three is a hard fight for levels 5–8; all six is far beyond deadly, and the GM should let the tableau's stillness say so. Joining the picture is leaving-something-behind in reverse; and the theme, literally: the fight on the cover never ended, and you only have to finish the ones you start.

Keyed areas

  • E1. The cave mouth. Arrival. The roper's gap (the thief).
  • E2. The ledge. The centaur's gap (the archer).
  • E3. The hoard. The dragon's gap (the fighter with the shield) and the treasure.
  • E4. The chest. The troll's gap (the dwarf).
  • E5. The back wall. The owlbear's gap (the cleric); the unicorn's gap (the elf) beside it.

Automation

Automated: each person-shaped gap whispers which monster wakes, once.

Bartleby Stickit, Bart to his friends (which is everyone who has drunk his cider twice). Keeper of the Stickit Inn, as his father was. Kind. Tired in a way that is not unhappy. He pours the house cider with a heavy hand, led the party up the stairs with a lantern and showed them the cots, and in the night he comes down the wrong stairwell with a tray.

Room 1. He tells them it is not morning yet and they should go back to bed; the road will be there tomorrow. He knows one detail about one character that the character has never told anyone. If pressed about it he does not understand the question.

Room 5. His voice from the common room below is the sound of ordinary morning.

Things They Say

  • Pouring. “House cider. Pressed in the yard, served cold. Goes down like water and gets up like a mule.”
  • Showing them upstairs. “Cot each, made up fresh. Bread on at first light, and a jug for the road. Mind the third step; it's been the third step since my father's day.”
  • The night, on the stone stairs. “Not morning yet. Back to bed, now. The road'll be there tomorrow. It always is.”
  • He knows (pick the detail before the session). “Your mother still keeps the lamp in the window, doesn't she? The blue one.”
  • If pressed about how he knows. “Know what, love? Drink your milk.”
  • If they go back to sleep. “There we are. I'll set another tray.”
  • Asked if he used to be a scrivener. (He nods.) But I'm not any more.
  • Asked why, or asked to write, copy or witness anything. “I would prefer not to.”
  • Room 5, from downstairs. “Are they up yet? Bread's going hard. Tell them the wagon's in the yard.”

A blank-faced copy of one character: the one with the fewest Misremembering changes so far (the corridor has taken the least from them). It steps out of the far door on the second pass through the Corridor Between. It has that character's sheet with every number halved and no name.

Running it. This block is a 5th-level adventurer halved and plays as written; or run the macro The Back Room: make the Echo of a character to make a halved copy of a real character. It acts right after the copied character. The full procedure is on the Room 3 journal, The Echo. It stops the moment the loop breaks.

Things They Say

  • It does not speak. It mouths whatever the character it copies said on their last turn, a moment late, without a sound.
  • When the loop breaks. Nothing. It is just not there any more.

The first party: each player's first-ever D&D character, as the table misremembers them — overpowered, cooler than they were, one running joke swollen into a whole personality. They are not hostile. They want the game to keep going, forever, with the party in it.

This table's five, built from the players' own answers: Fred the Fighter (in Room 2), Strider (in a Corridor at visit 7+), and Thon, Rorvik and T. Morlock, who wait with the others in the Hoard. The three fallbacks stand in if a player misses a session, or for another table.

Rules

  • Max hit points, never rolled.
  • The Signature always works, once per round.
  • Everything else is blank.
  • It never attacks first.
  • At 0 HP it stands back up in the pose it fell in.
  • It cannot leave a room through a door the party came through.

The map the Remnant hands over in Room 2 has an X on it. The X marks the way out. It moves when nobody looks at it. It points at the Hoard.
